text: Lesson three covered the roles administrators hand out: job, abstract, and data roles. This lesson goes one level deeper, to the building blocks those roles are made of — duty roles and privileges.

A duty role represents a set of related tasks, something granular like Accounts Payable Invoice Processing or Journal Entry Creation. This is the layer where function security privileges and data security policies actually attach. The design guideline is: grants go to duty roles, and duty roles get handed to job or abstract roles as children — not the reverse. A job role like Accounts Payable Manager doesn't hold privileges directly; it holds a set of duty roles.

A privilege is a single real world action on a single business object — create an invoice, approve a journal, void a payment. It secures the actual page, button, or process underneath. A privilege is granted to a duty role, never to a job role directly and never to a user directly. So read from the bottom up: privilege, to duty role, to job or abstract role, to user, through provisioning.

Duty roles aren't flat — one duty role can inherit other, more granular duty roles, so small well defined pieces of access get reused across multiple job roles instead of redefined each time. For you as a future consultant, that means when someone at Castellan Robotics can't do something specific, the fix is almost never adding a privilege straight to their account. It's tracing which duty role should carry it, confirming the job role includes that duty role, and confirming the job role is actually provisioned.

The chain is privilege, duty role, job or abstract role, user — and tracing that chain is the core skill for fixing access problems later in this course. Up next, lesson five: function security versus data security, in full depth.
